title: Trump Administration Weighs $100,000 Bond for Green Card Applicants Abroad
excerpt: The State Department is exploring whether it can require overseas green card seekers to post a refundable deposit of up to $100,000 before receiving an immigrant visa, expanding a bond pilot originally designed for tourist visas.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • The State Department plans a $100,000 bond for some overseas green card applicants.
  • Bonds are refundable only after applicants become US citizens, taking at least five years.
  • The proposal expands on a tourist visa bond pilot that has grown to 50 countries.
  • Indian families seeking green cards would be significantly impacted by this new requirement.
  • The State Department is developing a plan to require some overseas green card applicants to post a refundable bond of up to $100,000 before receiving an immigrant visa.
  • The bond would be returned only after the applicant becomes a US citizen, a process that takes at least five years.
  • The proposal builds on a tourist visa bond pilot that has expanded from two African countries to 50 since August 2025.
  • Indians seeking family-sponsored green cards through US consulates would be among the most affected, though specific countries have not been named.

The Trump administration is developing a plan to require some overseas green card applicants to post a refundable bond of up to $100,000 before receiving an immigrant visa, the Wall Street Journal reported, in the latest effort to restrict legal immigration to those the government deems financially self-sufficient.

The State Department is examining whether existing authorities under the Immigration and Nationality Act allow it to impose the requirement without new legislation. The initial rollout would target a limited number of countries through a pilot program before any broader expansion, according to people familiar with the discussions.

"President Trump has made clear that those who wish to immigrate to the United States must be financially self-sufficient."

— Tommy Pigott, State Department spokesperson

The department, Pigott said, is exploring bond requirements "as a way to demonstrate they have access to the funds needed to support themselves."

How the Bond Would Work

Under the proposal, applicants would need to deposit the bond before receiving an immigrant visa at a US consulate abroad. The amount would vary by case and could be higher or lower than the $100,000 benchmark. The government would return the funds only after the applicant becomes a US citizen — a process that takes at least five years after obtaining a green card.

The deposit would serve as collateral in case a green card holder turns to public assistance or fails to maintain financial independence. Family members would be permitted to post the bond on behalf of the primary applicant.

Building on the Tourist Visa Pilot

The green card proposal builds on a tourist visa bond pilot that the State Department has been running since August 2025. That program initially required applicants from Malawi and Zambia to post refundable bonds of up to $15,000, forfeited if they overstayed their visas or applied for another immigration status such as asylum.

The pilot has since expanded to 50 countries, most of them in Africa. The State Department has cited a 97 percent compliance rate among bond-posting travelers as evidence of the program's effectiveness. Officials eventually plan to extend the tourist visa bond requirement to all applicants outside the Visa Waiver Program, according to people familiar with the plans.

What It Means for Indian Families

A full rollout of the green card bond would hit Indians seeking family-sponsored green cards through US consulates particularly hard. India is among the largest sources of family-based immigration to the United States, and wait times for family-preference categories already stretch decades for Indian nationals.

Most employment-based applicants, including H-1B visa holders, already reside in the US and process their green cards domestically through adjustment of status, bypassing the overseas consulate route. The bond requirement would primarily affect family reunification cases — parents, siblings, and married children of US citizens and permanent residents who are still in India.

Sharvari Dalal-Dheini of the American Immigration Lawyers Association called the approach a "pay-for-play" system.

"Only the wealthy can come visit, or reunite with family, or seek a better life for themselves."

— Sharvari Dalal-Dheini, American Immigration Lawyers Association

Public Charge Rule Revived

The bond proposal arrived the same day the administration revived the so-called "public charge" rule, which allows green card denials for immigrants who use public benefits such as food stamps, Medicaid, and housing vouchers. The original version of the rule took effect during Trump's first term in 2020 but had limited impact because the pandemic halted most immigration processing.

The two moves together signal a coordinated push to tighten the financial threshold for legal immigration from multiple angles — both by screening applicants for past benefit use and by requiring them to prove future self-sufficiency through cash deposits.

What Comes Next

The green card bond remains in the discussion phase. Neither the specific countries nor the applicant categories that would be targeted first have been announced. The State Department would need to determine its legal authority under existing immigration law before launching the pilot, a step that could invite legal challenges from immigration advocacy groups.

For Indian families already navigating years-long visa backlogs and rising processing fees, a six-figure deposit requirement would add another formidable barrier to a system that many already view as increasingly hostile to legal immigration.
